# Inside the Mídas restoration: what the marks recover
Every name in this series was once flattened to fit a keyboard. **Mídas** is what the evidence put back.

The Greeks attached two great fables to Mídas — the touch and the ears — and one genuine history: the wealthy Phrygian king whose gifts reached Delphi and whose wars reached Assyria. Ovid gives the fables their classic form; Herodotus keeps the history. Silenos, the drunken companion of Dionysos, strayed and was brought to Mídas — in some tellings caught in the king's own rose gardens.  Mídas entertained him ten days and returned him to the god, who offered any gift in thanks.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Mídas
- **ASCII form:** midas
- **Meaning:** "Phrygian royal name"
- **Domain of influence:** King of Phrygia, the Golden Touch
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** Μίδας
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 152 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **Μίδας**. On the evidence, it means "Phrygian royal name".

Strip **Mídas** to *midas* and one piece of evidence vanishes:

- **i → í** — Acute on i: the stress position the ASCII form cannot show.

None of these marks is decoration. Each one is a fact about how the name was spoken, and each one is checkable against the scholarly record the temple cites.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Mídas** lives at [/sites/midas/](/sites/midas/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/midas/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/midas/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/midas/patterns/).

The restoration preserves one decisive feature the ASCII form drops — a single, honest mark — which places it in Tier-2: exact, and exactly labeled.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Mídas** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Finance, Wealth & Commerce** — Wealth personified — the name every gold fund wishes it owned.
- **Gems, Jewelry & Luxury Materials** — The golden touch itself; the precious metal made myth.
- **Agriculture, Food & Harvest** — Herodotus records the sixty-petaled roses of Phrygia — a horticultural legend (8.138).

This is the part of the file that surprises people: a four-thousand-year-old name, mapping cleanly onto twenty-first-century trades. The patterns are not marketing — they are the same myths, read forward.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Greek tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Theogony](/texts/theogony/), [Homeric Hymns](/texts/homeric-hymns/), and [Works and Days](/texts/works-and-days/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
